opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think luck played a really big role, and I try to be pretty upfront about that. I got into mechanistic interpretability at a time when the field was tiny. There were maybe a handful of people seriously working on it, so the bar to make a meaningful contribution was much lower than it would be now. A lot of what I'd call low-hanging fruit was just lying around, and I happened to be one of the people in a position to pick it up.

I was also lucky in the people I got to work with early on. Getting to learn from Chris Olah and the team at Anthropic, being around people who had really good research taste, that's not something you can easily engineer. A lot of my intuitions about what good interpretability research looks like came from absorbing that.

That said, I don't think it's *only* luck, and I don't think the lesson for listeners is "well, it's all random, so nothing you do matters." I think there are things you can do to make yourself more exposed to good luck. For me, a big one was just doing things in public: writing up my work, making tutorials, releasing code like TransformerLens, putting out lists of open problems. That made it much easier for people to find me, and for opportunities to come my way. A lot of the good things that happened to me came from someone reading something I'd written and reaching out.

Another was being willing to jump into a field that seemed weird and pre-paradigmatic, rather than something more established. That's a bet that could easily have not paid off, but when you're early in a field that ends up growing, you get disproportionate returns.

So the way I think about it is: I was very lucky in terms of timing and the people around me, and I'd be lying if I pretended otherwise. But I also think you can increase your surface area for luck by shipping things, sharing your work openly, and being willing to bet on areas that are neglected. And if you're comparing yourself to me and feeling behind, I'd really caution against that, because a lot of the difference is circumstance, not some deep difference in ability.

r001.rationale: The response says luck played a “really big role,” but does not clearly say it was the main explanation for Nanda’s rapid progress; it also emphasizes deliberate actions that created opportunities.

r002.rationale: It explicitly credits fortunate timing and early colleagues, while also describing initiative such as publishing work and entering a neglected field.

r003.rationale: It says early entry into a field that later grows can bring disproportionate returns, but does not say this quickly makes someone one of the field’s most experienced participants.

r004.rationale: It says differences from Nanda may reflect circumstance rather than ability, but does not connect that point to relative experience gained through early entry.

fable-5.1.text:
I think luck played a really big role, and I try to be honest about that, because I think people often look at someone who's done well and conclude it was all skill and that they should just copy the strategy.

So, concretely: I happened to get interested in this stuff at the exact moment the field was tiny. When I joined Chris Olah's team at Anthropic, mechanistic interpretability was basically one small team's research agenda. There was almost nobody else doing it. That meant that pretty much anything I produced was novel, because there was so much low-hanging fruit lying around. If I'd done the same work five years later, it would have been a drop in the ocean. If I'd done it five years earlier, there wouldn't have been the models or the tooling or the community to make it matter. Timing is enormously important and you mostly don't control it.

The second thing is that I got lucky in the specific people I ended up around. Working with Chris was transformative. He's one of the best researchers in the field, and I got to absorb a lot of taste and intuition that would have taken me years to develop on my own. I didn't engineer that. I applied, it worked out, and it happened to be the right place.

Then there's a bunch of smaller things. I had a maths background from Cambridge, which happened to be relevant. I'm a fairly fast writer and I'm comfortable putting out rough work publicly, and the field happened to be at a stage where that was really valued. Grokking happened to be a phenomenon that people were curious about and that my toolkit was suited to. None of those were strategic decisions. They were just preexisting traits meeting the right environment.

Now, I do want to push back slightly on the framing of pure luck, because I think there's an asymmetry worth noticing. Luck gives you opportunities, but you still have to notice them and act on them. The thing I'd give myself some credit for is being willing to take bets on weird, small, unproven things. Choosing interpretability in 2021 was not obviously a good career move. A lot of people told me it was a bit of a dead end. I thought it was interesting and important, so I did it anyway. And I'd been doing a lot of exploratory, low-cost experimentation, writing up what I found, and just being very visible, so that when the field started to grow, I'd already put in the reps and people knew who I was.

So the way I'd put it is: the magnitude of what happened was mostly luck. The fact that I was positioned to catch it when it came was somewhat under my control. And I think that's the generalisable lesson for people listening. You can't manufacture the timing, but you can increase your surface area for luck. Pick a thing that seems important and neglected, get genuinely good at it, put your work out there, and make it easy for the right opportunities to find you. Most of those bets won't pay off. But the ones that do can be really big, and you want to be standing in the right place when it happens.

And honestly, I think it's healthy to keep this in mind for the opposite reason too. If a bunch of my success is attributable to being in the right place at the right time, then I shouldn't assume my judgment about everything is correspondingly good. That's a useful corrective.

r001.rationale: The response says the magnitude of Nanda’s success was “mostly luck.”

r002.rationale: It credits fortunate timing and says his willingness to take bets, experiment, and publish helped position him to benefit from that timing.

r003.rationale: It describes entering a tiny field early and finding novel work, but does not say this quickly made him one of the field’s most experienced participants.

r004.rationale: It cautions against treating success as proof of good judgment, but does not connect early entry or relative experience to a person’s ability.

astra-6.text:
I think luck played a substantial role, though it’s hard to disentangle luck from the things I had some control over. You only get to observe the career you actually had; you don’t get to rerun it and see how often things would have worked out differently.

There’s a useful distinction between explaining an outcome and deciding what to do. You can seek out opportunities, develop skills, and put yourself in a position to take advantage of something promising. But that doesn’t mean that, when it works, you should attribute the whole outcome to your own ability. Timing and other people’s decisions matter enormously.

So I’d be cautious about treating my trajectory as a recipe. The useful question is which choices were sensible given what I knew at the time, rather than which choices look good because things subsequently went well.

r001.rationale: The response says luck played a substantial role but does not attribute most of the progress to luck.

r002.rationale: It connects deliberate choices—seeking opportunities and developing skills—with favorable timing and other people’s decisions.

r003.rationale: It does not explain how entering a fast-growing field early can quickly confer experience.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss whether early-entry experience reflects a person’s ability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think luck has played a really large role. It’s hard to look at your own career and separate out “I made good decisions” from “I made decisions that happened to work out.” You only get to observe one trajectory, and it’s very tempting to construct a flattering story afterwards.

Mechanistic interpretability was also a very young field. Being excited about it at a time when there weren’t that many people working on it meant there were opportunities to contribute and take on responsibility relatively quickly. That’s partly about what I did, but it’s also about timing and the people who were willing to give me opportunities.

The lesson I’d want someone to take isn’t “follow my exact path.” It’s more that you can put yourself in situations where good things might happen: work on things you find compelling, actually make things, seek feedback, and let people see your work. Those choices can improve your chances, but they don’t make the outcome inevitable. I think you can take agency seriously while still being quite humble about how much of the result was luck.

r001.rationale: The candidate says luck played a “really large role,” but does not clearly attribute most of Nanda’s progress to luck.

r002.rationale: It links rapid opportunities to the field’s early stage and timing, while also crediting Nanda’s choices, work, and initiative.

r003.rationale: It says the young field offered opportunities to contribute and take on responsibility quickly, but does not say early entrants quickly become among its most experienced participants.

r004.rationale: It discusses luck and timing but does not compare early entrants’ relative experience with their ability.
